html:
Ghalib was a poet of Delhi who wrote in Urdu and Persian, born in Agra in 1797. He is widely seen as the greatest master of the Urdu ghazal, a short love poem in rhymed couplets.

He moved to Delhi as a young man and lived there the rest of his life, in the last decades of the Mughal court. His ghazals are about love, loss and doubt, often with wit and a turn of irony in the second line. He never had steady wealth and spent years fighting for a family pension. All seven of his children died young.

He was close to the court of the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, himself a poet, who made him a court historian.

He lived through the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and the British sack of Delhi, which he recorded in a Persian diary, Dastanbuy, and in his letters. His letters, written in a lively, chatty Urdu prose, were new for their time and helped shape modern Urdu writing. He died in 1869. His couplets are still quoted and sung across India and Pakistan.
